lead: Real wing sections mix closed cells with open parts: a torque box with an open trailing-edge section behind the rear spar, or a box with a cut-out for an undercarriage bay. The closed cell can carry a constant circulating flow; the open part cannot, because it has a free edge. The method cuts each closed cell once, finds the open-section flow everywhere, adds one constant per cell, and fixes it from moment equilibrium or from the twist condition.
prereq: You need: the cut-and-add method of the closed-section chapter, the boom jumps of the idealisation chapter, and the twist-rate integral.

blocks.text: A mixed section has one or more closed cells and at least one open wall ending in a free edge. The open wall starts from q = 0 at its free edge, like any open section. The closed cell has no free edge, so it is cut once in imagination. After the cuts the whole section is open, and the basic flow q<sub>b</sub> is found from the free edges and the cuts, using the I<sub>xx</sub> of the whole section: every boom, open or closed, carries bending stress.

items: Compute I<sub>xx</sub> (and I<sub>yy</sub>, I<sub>xy</sub> if needed) for the whole section, open parts included.
Cut each closed cell once. Start q<sub>b</sub> at every free edge and at every cut with zero.
Sum the jumps at the booms (or integrate along walls that carry direct stress). Where an open wall joins a cell, its flow enters the cell at the junction boom.
Add one unknown constant q<sub>s,0</sub> to each closed cell. Open walls get no constant.
Fix the constants: moment equilibrium if the load position is known, zero twist if the shear centre is wanted.

blocks.text: S<sub>y</sub> x<sub>S</sub> = Σ (moments of q<sub>b</sub> about O) + Σ 2A<sub>R</sub> q<sub>s,0,R</sub>
blocks.where: x<sub>S</sub> is the distance of the load line from the moment point O (mm); A<sub>R</sub> is the area enclosed by cell R (mm²); the moment of a constant cell flow about any point is 2A<sub>R</sub> q<sub>s,0,R</sub>, anticlockwise positive.
the rate of twist (rad/mm), from cell R only; the open walls do not appear because they enclose no area.

blocks.text: The open walls do twist with the section; they just add almost nothing to the torsional stiffness, since their torsion constant is Σbt³/3 against the 4A²/∮ds/t of the cell. That is why the cell alone sets the rate of twist. With two cells sharing a wall, the twist integral for each cell uses the net flow in the shared wall, q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>s,0,1</sub> − q<sub>s,0,2</sub>, and the two rates are set equal, as in the multi-cell chapter.

sections.h3: When the load is not at the shear centre

blocks.text: If the load line is known, the moment equation gives the constant directly and the twist equation gives the rate of twist. If the shear centre is wanted, set the rate of twist to zero instead, solve for the constant, and put it into the moment equation to find x<sub>S</sub>. A load anywhere else twists the section by the amount the first approach gives. The trailing panels of a wing behind the rear spar move the shear centre slightly aft, because their small flows add a moment, but they hardly change the torsional stiffness.

figure.caption: The worked mixed section, booms drawn to scale. The trailing panels start from zero at the free booms 5 and 6 and carry 6.90 N/mm; only the closed cell gets a constant, q<sub>s,0</sub> = −27.59 N/mm, fixed by moments about the loaded front spar. The shear centre is 99.1 mm behind the front spar, so the load twists the section nose up.

spec.aria: A rectangular cell with booms 1 and 2 on top, 4 and 3 below, and two thin trailing panels from booms 2 and 3 converging to free booms 5 and 6. Arrows show 68.97 newtons per millimetre up the front spar, 34.48 up the rear spar, 27.59 clockwise in the top and bottom skins and 6.90 in each trailing panel. A 10 kilonewton upward load acts on the front spar; the shear centre S is marked 99.1 millimetres behind it. A note gives q nought as minus 27.59 and the twist as 0.482 degrees per metre, nose up.

examples.question: A wing section is idealised into six booms. The closed cell has booms 1 (0, 50), 2 (200, 50), 3 (200, −50) and 4 (0, −50) mm with areas 600, 800, 800 and 600 mm²; its spar webs are 2 mm and its skins 1.5 mm thick. Two open trailing panels run from booms 2 and 3 to booms 5 (300, 25) and 6 (300, −25), each 200 mm², which are free edges. A shear S<sub>y</sub> = 10 kN acts along the front spar (x = 0). With G = 27 GPa, find the shear flows, the rate of twist and the shear centre.
steps: Open panels, from the free booms: q₅₂ = −0.001379 × 200 × 25 = −6.90 N/mm (from 5 to 2); q₆₃ = +6.90 N/mm (from 6 to 3).
Cut the top skin 2–1. From boom 1 down the front spar: q₁₄ = −0.001379 × 600 × 50 = −41.38 N/mm. Boom 4 (y = −50) cancels it: q₄₃ = 0.
Boom 3 receives q₆₃ and adds −k × 800 × (−50): q₃₂ = 0 + 6.90 + 55.17 = 62.07 N/mm up the rear spar. At boom 2, 62.07 + (−6.90) − 55.17 = 0, which matches the cut.
Check: vertical forces 4,138 (front) + 6,207 (rear) − 2 × 172.4 (trailing panels) = 10,000 N = S<sub>y</sub>.

Moments about O, the front spar mid-point, anticlockwise positive: rear spar 200 × 6,207 = 1,241,379; each trailing panel −68,966; total 1,103,448 N·mm. The load passes through O, so 0 = 1,103,448 + 2 × 20,000 q<sub>s,0</sub> and q<sub>s,0</sub> = −27.59 N/mm.
Final cell flows: front spar −68.97 (that is 68.97 upwards), bottom skin −27.59, rear spar 34.48, top skin −27.59 N/mm; trailing panels ±6.90 N/mm.
Twist: ∮q ds/t = −9,080 N/mm, so dθ/dz = −9,080/(2 × 20,000 × 27,000) = −8.41 × 10⁻⁶ rad/mm = −0.482°/m, that is 0.482°/m clockwise (nose up for lift on the front spar).

Shear centre: zero twist gives q<sub>s,0</sub> = −∮q<sub>b</sub> ds/t ÷ ∮ds/t = −1,034.5/366.67 = −2.821 N/mm, and x<sub>S</sub> = (1,103,448 + 40,000 × −2.821)/10,000 = 99.1 mm behind the front spar.
examples.answer: q<sub>s,0</sub> = −27.59 N/mm; front spar 68.97 N/mm, rear spar 34.48 N/mm, skins 27.59 N/mm, trailing panels 6.90 N/mm; rate of twist 0.482° per metre, nose up; shear centre 99.1 mm behind the front spar.

traps: Treating the whole section as one closed tube. The trailing panels have a free edge and enclose nothing.
Leaving the open booms out of I<sub>xx</sub>. They carry bending stress and change every q<sub>b</sub>.
Adding q<sub>s,0</sub> to the open panels. A constant flow can only circulate round a closed cell.
Saying the open part does not twist. It twists with the section; it simply adds almost no torsional stiffness and no twist equation of its own.

quiz.q: Where does the shear flow start in a mixed section?
quiz.a: At zero at every free edge of the open walls, and at zero at the imaginary cut in each closed cell (with q<sub>s,0</sub> added later).

quiz.q: Why does the closed cell alone set the rate of twist of the mixed section?
quiz.a: The rate of twist comes from ∮q ds/t round an enclosed area. The open panels enclose no area, and their own torsion constant Σbt³/3 is tiny beside 4A²/∮ds/t of the cell.

quiz.q: In the example, find the final flow in the rear spar.
In the example, what torque about the shear centre does the load cause?
quiz.a: The load is 99.1 mm ahead of the shear centre: T = 10,000 × 99.1 = 990,596 N·mm, which the cell carries as an extra Bredt–Batho flow of 24.76 N/mm.

quiz.q: What happens to the shear centre if the trailing booms are made larger?
quiz.a: The trailing panels carry more flow, their moment about the front spar grows, and the shear centre moves aft. The cell constant at zero twist changes too, so the shift must be recomputed, not guessed.

quiz.q: A torque box has a cut-out that removes the bottom skin over one bay. How does the bay carry torque?
quiz.a: Over the bay the section is open: no closed cell, so no Bredt–Batho flow. The torque must be carried by the much weaker St Venant torsion of the open walls, or by differential bending of the spars, with the ribs at each end of the cut-out redistributing the flow. The cut-out bay is far more flexible and needs local reinforcement.

beyond: Not for the exam. Undercarriage bays, access panels and fuel-tank doors make cut-outs in real boxes, and the redistribution of shear flow around them is a standard stress-office check. Search for "cut-outs in wing boxes shear flow".
